plan.contextChunk: This figure sets four triangle sketches in a row, labeled (a) through (d) below, to enumerate the possible outcomes when two sides and a non-included angle are known. All four share one labeling scheme: an acute angle alpha marked by an arc at the left end of a horizontal base, a vertex beta at the right end of that base, an apex gamma above, side b rising from alpha to gamma, and side a hanging from gamma. Panel (a), headed No triangle, a < h, draws a as a short vertical segment from gamma that stops above the base, leaving a visible gap so nothing closes. Panel (b), headed Right triangle, a = h, has a reaching the base exactly at beta, with a small square marking the right angle formed there. Panel (c), headed Two triangles, a > h, a < b, shows a solid vertical altitude labeled h from gamma to the base, plus two dashed segments each labeled a running from gamma to different landing points, one to the left of the altitude's foot and one at beta. Panel (d), headed One triangle, a is greater than or equal to b, shows a broad triangle whose side a slopes from gamma down to beta. Aligning the four under identical labels isolates the one quantity that changes, the length of a measured against the altitude and against b, and shows how many closures each case admits.

demo_steps.title: Too short: no triangle
demo_steps.narration: With a shorter than the altitude h, the candidate side from gamma cannot reach the base. The visible gap shows why no triangle can close.

demo_steps.title: Exactly the altitude: right triangle
demo_steps.narration: When a equals h, the side reaches the base at exactly one point: the foot of the perpendicular. That creates one right triangle.

demo_steps.title: Between h and b: two triangles
demo_steps.narration: When a is longer than h but still shorter than b, it can swing to meet the base in two different places. These two landings produce two distinct triangles.

demo_steps.title: At least as long as b: one triangle
demo_steps.narration: Once a is at least as long as b, the second possible landing disappears, leaving only one triangle.

demo_steps.title: Hide the guide, then restore it
demo_steps.narration: Turning the altitude guide off leaves only the triangle sketches; turning it back on reveals the threshold that organizes all four cases.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: For the SSA ambiguous case with acute alpha, the altitude h is the reach threshold and b is the one-versus-two threshold.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Recreate the original as four horizontally aligned black-line geometric panels on a white background, with serif italic math labels alpha, beta, gamma, a, b, and h. Use a fixed acute angle alpha and fixed side b in all panels; normalize b to about 1 and h = b sin(alpha) to about 0.6 for the slider logic. Keep the base horizontal, alpha at the left, gamma above, and side b slanting upward from alpha to gamma. Use solid black lines for actual triangle sides, dashed black lines for alternate possible a positions in the two-triangle case, and a small square to mark right angles when the altitude is shown. The slider should visually swing or extend side a from gamma toward the base and automatically emphasize the matching panel; the case-step control should set representative values of a and add a subtle colored highlight around the relevant panel plus a brighter highlight on the gap, right angle, dashed alternatives, or final single side.

authoredContext:
Oblique triangles in the category SSA may have four different outcomes. The figure illustrates the solutions with the known sides a and b and known angle α.

Four attempted oblique triangles are in a row, all with standard labels. Side c is the horizontal base. In the first attempted triangle, side a is less than the altitude height. Since side a cannot reach side c, there is no triangle. In the second attempted triangle, side a is equal to the length of the altitude height, so side a forms a right angle with side c. In the third attempted triangle, side a is greater than the altitude height and less than side b, so side a can form either an acute or obtuse angle with side c. In the fourth attempted triangle, side a is greater than or equal to side b, so side a forms an acute angle with side c.
